Lessons.Title: Situations Involving Equal-size Groups
ExplanationParagraphs:
Learning goal: You will solve division problems in context, and to recall the two meanings of division: “how many in each group” and “how many groups.
In grade 3, you learned about the relationship between multiplication and division and reasoned about division in terms of equal groups. You also saw two interpretations of division: as a way to find the size of a group and as a way to find the number of groups. You used these understandings to find quotients and to reason about division problems in context, finding whole-number quotients from two-digit dividends and one-digit divisors.
Core relationship: Situations with equal-size groups. Use multiplication or division consistently for the total, number of groups or group size.

Local publisher 2021 source lesson activities: Warm-up: Estimation Exploration: Lots of Paletas	 (10 minutes); Activity 1:  Paletas for a Class Party	 (15 minutes); Activity 2: More Snacks for a Class Party (20 minutes); Cool-down:  After the Class Party	 (5 minutes)
Source-aligned Edulytics model: A class of 24 students receives three paletas each. How many paletas?
First-party Cool-down (not gated original): Forty-eight paletas are packed 6 per box. How many boxes?
Original visual/physical and peer-explanation activities still require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Situations with equal-size groups
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use multiplication or division consistently for the total, number of groups or group size.
KeyConcepts.Example: A class of 24 students receives three paletas each. How many paletas?

KeyConcepts.Title: Exact task method
KeyConcepts.Definition: Division can ask how many equal groups or how many items in each group.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Division can ask how many equal groups or how many items in each group.
KeyConcepts.Example: Ninety-six counters are put in equal groups of eight. How many groups?

KeyConcepts.Title: Independent partial-product check
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use inverse multiplication to check a quotient.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use inverse multiplication to check a quotient.
KeyConcepts.Example: One hundred forty-four tiles are shared equally among twelve groups. How many in each?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choosing multiplication when the total is being partitioned into equal groups.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It changes the unit, place value, or operation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use multiplication or division consistently for the total, number of groups or group size.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing the number of groups with the size of each group.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The chosen operation or representation does not match the stated context.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State which quantity the divisor represents.
